newsitem.title: INDIA: RBI policy "mildly favorable" for stocks - Paribas.
newsitem.headline: RBI policy "mildly favorable" for stocks - Paribas.

text.p: Paribas Capital Markets strategist Rupa Bose issued the following commentary on measures announced today in the Reserve Bank of India's half year credit policy statement;

Though the slack season credit policy announced today does not appear to have an immediate effect on equities, its provisions are consonant with the favorable directions set by the previous policy. We consider it mildly favourable for the stock market. The only move that might have a direct impact is a small change in the ceiling regulations on bank investments in the stock market. It may also help lower real interest rate expectations, which would again tend to favour equities.

The slack season credit policy is trying to reduce interest rates, and ease some of the restrictions on the money market. Many of these will make life easier for banks, and indirectly for corporations. We do not think this has a direct impact on the equity market; most of the moves here are designed to bring (down) interest rates reflect the easier money conditions that have existed following the last credit policy. In particular, the RBI reference rate has been lowered one percentage point, and so has the ceiling on interest paid on deposits in banks.
One signal that foreign exchange inflows have probably been strong:

The RBI has reimposed the reserve requirement on non-resident foreign currency deposits (FCNR). This in turn means that at present, there is no downward pressure on the exchange rate. Banks will very likely slow their marketing efforts on these deposits.
Interbank lendings have been exempted from reserve requirements:

This will simplify bank operations; they used to lend (or borrow) for 13 days at a time, to avoid having the interbank loans outstanding on the alternate Fridays used to compute reserve requirements. The new rule means that the artificial 'break' every 13 days is no longer necessary.
Companies should find it easier to get money; many irritations in the system have been eliminated:

Commercial paper, which could only be issued for over 90 days, may now be issued for 30 days or more. Banks do not have to form consortia lend to companies (this was formely required for loans above 500 million rupees). Non-banking financial institutions also may borrow from banks as much as banks are willing to lend them; ceilings that earlier applied have been abolished. Companies may also borrow money from banks against shares, (which banks may lend them subject to the 5 percent ceiling.)

Banks are allowed to invest up to 5 percent of their incremental deposits each year in stocks. Earlier, this included preference shares, debentures, and corporate bonds as well as common stock. Now, the ceiling applies to ordinary shares only.
To the extent that this policy lowers interest rates, it may make equity more interesting for retail investors:

This would be determined by nominal interest rates on available opportunities, and on inflation expectations. The maximum they can now get in bank deposits is 9 percent; the RBI targets inflation at 6 percent, but many consider about 8-9 percent more realistic. Depending on whether investors find opportunities in direct lending to the corporate sector (i.e., "company deposits") - and we think these opportunities could shrink significantly as companies find easier ways to get money - retail investors may find the equity market promises stronger real returns.
